WATTS CHARGES AND EPSTEIN CREDITS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Watts Charges and Epstein Credits Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan, who separated on March 1, 2026 and whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Alameda County. It describes two related California case-law doctrines that can arise when such a proceeding remains pending after the date of separation but before trial or settlement: a "Watts charge," under which a spouse who has exclusive use of a community property asset after separation may be required to reimburse the community for the reasonable value of that use, and an "Epstein credit," under which a spouse who uses separate property funds to pay a preexisting community debt after separation may be entitled to reimbursement from the community for those payments. This information sheet states what California case law and the Family Code say about these two doctrines in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that either doctrine applies to Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan's specific property, debts, or circumstances; whether a Watts charge or Epstein credit applies in a particular case, and in what amount, is a matter for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan to resolve by their own written agreement.

WATTS CHARGES — REIMBURSEMENT FOR A SPOUSE'S EXCLUSIVE POST-SEPARATION USE OF A COMMUNITY ASSET
California case law recognizes that where one spouse has had the exclusive use of a community property asset — such as the family residence — after the date of separation and before trial, a court has the authority to require that spouse to reimburse the community for the reasonable value of that exclusive use. This reimbursement is commonly called a "Watts charge," after the Court of Appeal decision recognizing it. A Watts charge is not automatic: whether to order one, and in what amount, is a determination the trial court makes after considering all the circumstances under which exclusive use or possession came about.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "We hold that the trial court erred in concluding that it had no authority to reimburse the community for the value of John’s exclusive use of the family residence and the medical practice between the date of separation and the date of trial."
  — In re Marriage of Watts, 171 Cal.App.3d 366, 374 (1985) (California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District; opinion text via CourtListener), a spouse may be required to reimburse the community for the value of exclusive post-separation use of a community asset (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2127055/in-re-marriage-of-watts/)
  "Upon remand, the trial court will determine whether John should be required to reimburse the community for the value of his use of community assets after the date of separation in accordance with its findings. That determination should be made after taking into account all the circumstances under which exclusive possession was ordered."
  — In re Marriage of Watts, 171 Cal.App.3d 366, 374 (1985) (California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District; opinion text via CourtListener), reimbursement is a discretionary, fact-specific determination on remand, not an automatic order (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2127055/in-re-marriage-of-watts/)
  "The present case does not involve the use of separate property to pay community debts, and instead involves the reimbursement to the community for the exclusive use of a community property asset by one spouse."
  — In re Marriage of Watts, 171 Cal.App.3d 366, 373 (1985) (California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District; opinion text via CourtListener), Watts distinguishes exclusive-use reimbursement from reimbursement for separate funds used to pay community debts (the Epstein-credit doctrine) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2127055/in-re-marriage-of-watts/)
  Known gap: This is real California case law, used as evidence of what a published Court of Appeal decision actually held about a court's authority to charge a spouse for exclusive post-separation use of a community asset — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a Watts charge will be ordered, or in what amount, in any specific case. All three citations below are drawn from the same case, In re Marriage of Watts (1985) 171 Cal.App.3d 366 — different passages of the same opinion, not independent corroborating sources. Watts itself distinguishes this exclusive-use-reimbursement doctrine from the separate doctrine, addressed in this document's companion clauses, concerning a spouse's use of separate funds to pay community debts after separation (an Epstein credit) — the third quotation below is Watts's own statement of that distinction. This document does not address how a court values the "reasonable value of use" in a particular case (for example, by fair rental value), which Watts itself left to the trial court's factual determination on remand.

EPSTEIN CREDITS — REIMBURSEMENT FOR A SPOUSE'S USE OF SEPARATE FUNDS TO PAY A COMMUNITY DEBT AFTER SEPARATION
California case law recognizes that, although a spouse who uses separate property to pay a community obligation during marriage is generally not entitled to reimbursement absent an agreement, that no-reimbursement rule does not apply once the spouses have separated. The California Supreme Court has held that, as a general rule, a spouse who, after separation, uses earnings or other separate funds to pay a preexisting community obligation — such as a mortgage payment on the family residence — should be reimbursed for those payments from the community property upon dissolution. This reimbursement is commonly called an "Epstein credit," after the Supreme Court decision recognizing it. Reimbursement under this rule is not automatic; it is subject to exceptions addressed in this document's companion clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "we agree with the conclusion of In re Marriage of Smith, and adopt as the view of this court the following portion of the Court of Appeal opinion of Justice Kaufman"
  — In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 84 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener), the Supreme Court expressly adopts the reimbursement rule from In re Marriage of Smith as its own holding (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1410957/in-re-marriage-of-epstein/)
  "as a general rule, a spouse who, after separation of the parties, uses earnings or other separate funds to pay preexisting community obligations should be reimbursed therefor out of the community property upon dissolution. However, there are a number of situations in which reimbursement is inappropriate, so reimbursement should not be ordered automatically."
  — In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 84-85 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener), the general rule: separate funds used after separation to pay a preexisting community obligation should be reimbursed from the community upon dissolution (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1410957/in-re-marriage-of-epstein/)
  Known gap: This is real California Supreme Court case law, used as evidence of what the court actually held about reimbursement for separate funds used to pay community debts after separation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that an Epstein credit will be awarded, or in what amount, in any specific case. Both citations below are drawn from the same case, In re Marriage of Epstein (1979) 24 Cal.3d 76 — different passages of the same opinion (the Supreme Court's own statement adopting the rule, and its statement of the rule itself), not independent corroborating sources. The Supreme Court adopted this rule from a Court of Appeal decision, In re Marriage of Smith (1978) 79 Cal.App.3d 725, quoting that decision's language directly rather than restating it; this document cites Epstein, where the language became binding California Supreme Court authority, rather than Smith itself.

LIMITS ON EPSTEIN CREDITS — WHEN REIMBURSEMENT SHOULD NOT BE ORDERED
The reimbursement rule described in this document's companion clause is not automatic. California case law identifies several circumstances in which reimbursement for a spouse's post-separation payment of a community debt should not be ordered: where the parties agreed the payment would not be reimbursed, where the paying spouse truly intended the payment as a gift, where the payment was made on account of a debt for acquiring or preserving an asset the paying spouse was using and the amount paid was not substantially more than the value of that use, or where the payment in reality discharged the paying spouse's duty to support the other spouse or a dependent child.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Reimbursement should not be ordered if payment was made under circumstances in which it would have been unreasonable to expect reimbursement, for example, where there was an agreement between the parties the payment would not be reimbursed or where the paying spouse truly intended the payment to constitute a gift"
  — In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 84 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener), reimbursement should not be ordered where there was an agreement not to reimburse, or the payment was intended as a gift (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1410957/in-re-marriage-of-epstein/)
  "payment was made on account of a debt for the acquisition or preservation of an asset the paying spouse was using and the amount paid was not substantially in excess of the value of the use."
  — In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 85 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener), reimbursement should not be ordered where the amount paid was not substantially in excess of the value of the paying spouse's use of the asset (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1410957/in-re-marriage-of-epstein/)
  "Likewise, reimbursement should not be ordered where the payment on account of a preexisting community obligation constituted in reality a discharge of the paying spouse’s duty to support the other spouse or a dependent child of the parties."
  — In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 85 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener), reimbursement should not be ordered where the payment in reality discharged the paying spouse's duty of spousal or child support (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1410957/in-re-marriage-of-epstein/)
  Known gap: This is the same case cited in this document's companion clause on the Epstein-credit general rule — In re Marriage of Epstein (1979) 24 Cal.3d 76 — a different, adjoining passage of the same opinion (the exceptions the Supreme Court adopted alongside the general rule), not an independent corroborating source. The first two quotations below are split into separate citation entries only because a page break in the official reporter falls between them, not because they come from different sources. This document does not address the support-obligation exception's own sub-questions (for example, whether the spouses separated "by agreement" within the meaning of former Civil Code section 5131), which the Epstein opinion itself left for the trial court to determine on remand.

STATUTORY CODIFICATION — FAMILY CODE SECTION 2626
The California Legislature has given the family court express statutory jurisdiction to order the kind of post-separation reimbursement described in this document's companion clauses on Epstein credits: a court has jurisdiction to order reimbursement, in cases it deems appropriate, for debts paid after separation but before trial.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The court has jurisdiction to order reimbursement in cases it deems appropriate for debts paid after separation but before trial."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2626 (California Legislative Information text), the court's statutory jurisdiction to order reimbursement for debts paid after separation but before trial (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2626.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's codification of post-separation reimbursement jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This is a single statutory section (Family Code § 2626); no additional independent statutory source was found for it. By its own text, § 2626 speaks to reimbursement for "debts paid after separation but before trial" — squarely the Epstein-credit side of this document. No comparable Family Code provision was located that specifically codifies reimbursement for a spouse's exclusive post-separation use of a community asset (the Watts-charge side of this document); that doctrine, as far as this research could confirm, remains case law rather than a codified statutory rule, and this document does not claim otherwise.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Oakland, California.
